summary: Specifies new FTP commands for getting directory listings in a defined format and for restarting interrupted data transfers in STREAM mode. It also allows character sets other than US-ASCII and defines an optional virtual file storage structure. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Old file-sending commands were messy. These new ones give neat file lists computers can read and let a download pick up where it stopped, and they allow letters from other languages.

questions: how to resume an interrupted ftp transfer
how does ftp rest resume a transfer
what is the ftp size command
subtitle: New FTP commands for machine-readable directory listings, file sizes and times, and restarting interrupted transfers.

tldr.problem: FTP's directory listings had no defined format, and the original specification gave no way to restart an interrupted transfer in STREAM mode, although servers had long done it anyway.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3659 adds SIZE, MDTM, MLST and MLSD, defines how REST works in STREAM mode, and describes an optional tree-shaped file naming scheme called TVFS. Listings use a strict format of name=value facts followed by a pathname.
tldr.outcome: Clients can parse listings reliably and resume transfers from an octet offset. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 959.

facts.label: Standard facts
facts.value: 9 (size, modify, create, type, unique, perm, lang, media-type, charset)

today: RFC 3659 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2007. It updates RFC 959, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
RFC 3659 updates the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) from RFC 959. It adds four commands, SIZE, MDTM, MLST and MLSD, and modifies the existing REST command. The RFC says SIZE, MDTM and the REST changes had already been in wide use for many years, while the other two are new.

Together they let a client restart an interrupted transfer in transfer modes not previously supported in any documented way, and get a directory listing in a machine-friendly, predictable format. An optional structure for the server's file store, a Trivial Virtual File Store (TVFS), lets servers describe their naming rules to clients.
sections.eli5: FTP is a way to send files between computers. This document adds a few new commands so computers can ask better questions about files and keep going after a break.

sections.title: Conventions: Pathnames, Times and Replies
sections.content:
The RFC uses ABNF for its syntax and defines a few shared pieces. A time-val is 14 digits in the form YYYYMMDDHHMMSS, optionally followed by a period and decimal fractions of a second. Times are always UTC in the Gregorian calendar, and an implementation MUST NOT add precision that the underlying value does not have.

Pathnames are sent either as UTF-8 or as a raw string that is not valid UTF-8. The sender chooses, and the receiver should keep and retransmit the name unchanged. Pathnames containing the CR LF pair cannot be sent over a data connection, so such files must have the sequence converted reversibly or be omitted from listings.

For the commands defined here, pathnames are literal. No wildcard or pattern matching is allowed, so a client that wants matching must fetch a listing and filter it itself.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on one exact way to write a date and time, and file names are treated like labels exactly as written, with no guessing games or wildcards.

sections.title: MDTM, SIZE and Restarting with REST
sections.content:
MDTM returns a file's last modification time in a 213 reply, or a 550 reply if the time is unavailable. A client can compare it before and after an interruption to decide whether the source file changed, which would make a restart unsafe.

SIZE returns the exact number of octets that would be sent over the data connection under the current STRU, MODE and TYPE. The RFC's example shows a file of 1830 octets reported as 1942 under TYPE A because 112 line-end octets must be added. Estimates MUST NOT be returned. Because precision can be costly, clients should use it only when it is essential, such as before a restart.

In STREAM mode the data is unformatted octets, so no restart marker can be embedded. Instead the restart point is the octet offset: REST followed by a number tells the server how many octets of the next transfer to skip. The server answers 350, and the next command should be RETR or STOR. REST 0 turns restart off. REST used for anything other than completing an earlier failed transfer has undefined results.
sections.eli5: If a download stops halfway, the client counts how much it already has and says, start again from here. It can also ask the server how big or how old a file is, to check nothing changed.

sections.title: Trivial Virtual File Store (TVFS)
sections.content:
Servers often present a UNIX-like tree of directories. TVFS is an optional, named way to say so. In TVFS no elementary file name contains /, names are not empty (except the unnamed root), and names are sent as UTF-8. A fully qualified pathname begins with / and works from any current directory, while a relative pathname works only from a suitable directory. The path / alone refers to the root.

TVFS defines only naming. It adds no commands and guarantees no access control or other file properties. A server shows support by putting a line beginning TVFS in its FEAT reply, and it MUST NOT do so unless it implements TVFS as defined.
sections.eli5: TVFS is like agreeing that every file has an address such as /A/C/P, built from folder names joined by slashes, so you can name a file without walking to its folder first.

sections.title: MLST and MLSD Listings
sections.content:
MLST returns facts about exactly one named file or directory over the control connection, with no data connection. MLSD lists the contents of a directory over a data connection, and replies 501 if the name is not a directory. With no argument, they use the current directory.

Each entry is a series of name=value; facts, then exactly one space, then the pathname. The facts contain no spaces. The format is rigid: no headers, no extra spaces, no blank lines. The MLSD data connection behaves as if TYPE L 8, MODE S and STRU F were set, without changing those settings, and there is no maximum line length.

The standard facts are size, modify, create, type, unique, perm, lang, media-type and charset. Servers SHOULD support at least type, perm, size, unique and modify. Servers MUST NOT guess lang or media-type values.

The type fact is file, cdir (the listed directory), pdir (a parent directory), dir, or an operating-system-specific type. The perm fact is a set of letters, for example r for RETR and l for listing. These are a guide only and never promise a command will work. The size fact is approximate, so use SIZE when precision is needed.
sections.eli5: Each line is like a label on a box: a few short facts such as size, kind and when it changed, then the name. Every line looks the same way so a computer can read it without guessing.

sections.title: Feature Announcement and Fact Selection
sections.content:
Servers advertise support in the reply to FEAT (from RFC 2389). Support for MDTM and SIZE is shown by a line with that word, and restart in STREAM mode by exactly REST STREAM. For listings, a single MLST line lists the available facts. A trailing asterisk marks the facts returned by default. There is no separate line for MLSD.

A client can narrow the output with OPTS MLST followed by the fact names it wants. Facts not listed MUST NOT be returned, and unsupported ones are silently omitted. The choice applies to both MLST and MLSD. Clients are advised to be careful with facts outside the server's default set, because some are expensive to compute.
sections.eli5: Before asking, a client can say what the server knows how to do, and then pick only the facts it cares about, so the server does not do extra work.

sections.title: Character Sets, IANA and Security
sections.content:
Section 8 says that if MLST is supported, commands that take file names (such as CWD, RETR, STOR and DELE) must handle more than US-ASCII, treating names as in section 2. Pathnames are expected to be UTF-8, while FTP commands themselves remain ASCII. The RFC places no restrictions on file contents.

The IANA is asked to keep two new registries, for operating-system-specific facts and for operating-system-specific file types. The security section says the memo does not directly concern security, but notes that SIZE and some facts can load a server enough to enable denial of service. Servers should avoid revealing sensitive information, and a file system identifier that can bypass protections is not a suitable basis for the unique fact. FEAT and OPTS may be used before authentication, but MLSx commands may not.
sections.eli5: File names can use letters from many languages. Asking for exact sizes can make a busy server work hard, and servers should not give away secrets about files to strangers.

items.label: File
items.desc: A file entry containing non-system data.

items.label: Current directory
items.desc: The directory whose contents are listed; only returned by MLSD when the type fact is included.

items.label: Parent directory
items.desc: A parent of the listed directory.

items.label: OS-specific
items.desc: A file type that depends on the operating system or file system.
